Well, hi. Thanks for seeing me. I... I guess I'm here because things at work have just become completely untenable, and it's been weighing on me heavily. I'm a music director and composer, and for almost two years now—basically ever since this big commission I had, which was supposed to be this huge milestone for me after grad school—I’ve been completely unable to shake the certainty that a few people in the ensemble are actively trying to sabotage me. 

And I know how that sounds, but it's true, I see it happening every week. They started doing these things to quietly undermine my work, and it's so incredibly calculated. It's not out in the open where a guest conductor or the audience would catch it. It’s in the logistics. They’ll use sudden schedule changes right before a critical run-through, or they'll mess with the seating choices. And if you know anything about orchestration, you know that moving a principal player even a few feet completely alters the acoustic balance of the room, which they know I'm absolutely meticulous about. 

Then there are these little comments in rehearsals, just these tiny, targeted remarks masked as innocent questions about the score or the tempo. Just enough to plant doubt in the rest of the players. And the most frustrating part—the part that really gets to me and why I just can't let this go—is that whenever I try to address it, they always have this perfect cover. They’ll pull up these meticulously timed emails or administrative notes that supposedly explain the changes as just unavoidable conflicts or venue protocols. They show me this whole paper trail to make it look like it's just standard administrative shuffling, but I know exactly what they are actually doing, and it's been going on for two years...

Well, I... I don't really know how to answer that, to be perfectly honest, because... well, I've never been anything else. I mean, I've been studying music since I was six years old, sitting at the piano for hours on end, and through undergrad and grad school, my entire identity has just been completely wrapped up in this. Being a composer and a director, it's not just a job for me, it's the entire lens through which I interact with the world. 

So, if I weren't in this position, would they still target me? I don't know. I really don't. Because if I weren't the director, I wouldn't be in a position of authority over them, right? The whole dynamic would be completely different. The hierarchy of an ensemble is so incredibly rigid—you have the director at the top, making the final calls on interpretation, tempo, dynamics, everything, and then the section leaders, and so on. If I were just some guy working in an office somewhere, or even just a third-chair player in the back, they wouldn't have any reason to care about what I do. 

It's the fact that I'm the one holding the baton, the one whose name is on the score for this commission. That's what this is all about. They resent that a twenty-six-year-old is the one dictating the artistic vision. So, I guess I haven't really thought about it in a vacuum like that, because it's impossible to separate me from the music. The sabotage is specifically about the work. It's about ruining the performance and undermining my authority on the podium. If I weren't making music, there'd be nothing for them to ruin, you know? So I just don't see how the two could ever be separated.

I... I mean, I feel like we're just going around in circles here. Didn't we just cover this? You're asking me again if I'm misinterpreting things, just phrased a little differently. I look at a score and I see how the motifs connect, how the underlying harmony dictates the surface-level dissonance. I know how to look at evidence and draw a logical conclusion. 

And the conclusion—the only conclusion that actually fits all the data—is that this is intentional. If it were just one time that the principal cellist "forgot" his bowing markings, sure. I'd say he had a bad day. If it were just one time that the rehearsal space was double-booked right when we needed to finalize the phrasing in the second movement, fine. Administrative error. It's the way they always have an excuse ready, a perfectly plausible, printed-out excuse, before I even have a chance to ask what went wrong. 

You don't prepare a defense unless you know you're committing an offense, right? That's just human nature. If they were just making innocent mistakes, they'd be surprised when I brought it up. They'd say, "Oh, my bad, let's fix it." But they never say that. They immediately get defensive, they pull out the emails, they point the finger at the stage manager or the acoustics or the university scheduling office. It's a coordinated defense mechanism. 

So, no, I don't think it's possible that I'm just interpreting their actions that way. I'm observing their actions. I'm experiencing the direct result of their actions, which is the systemic sabotage of my music. And I just... I really need you to hear that. I need you to understand that I'm not making this up out of thin air. It's happening, and it's been happening for two years, and it's exhausting trying to convince people that I'm actually seeing what's right in front of me.

Losing my grip on reality? I... no. No, I really don't think so. I mean, I understand why you might ask that, because, sure, stress can do terrible things to a person's mind, and this whole situation has been incredibly stressful. But my grip on reality is exactly why I'm sitting here talking to you right now. 

I'm here because for almost two years now—basically ever since the ink dried on that commission—I have been completely unable to shake the certainty of what's happening. And it's not just some vague, paranoid feeling, it's an absolute certainty that a few specific people in the ensemble started actively, but very quietly, undermining my work. And they do it in these ways that are so deeply calculated. It's the schedule changes, like I mentioned before, but it's also things like seating choices. People outside of music don't realize how much seating matters, but if you put a dominant player in the wrong chair or split up a desk that usually plays together, it completely throws off the section's acoustic balance, and they know that. They know exactly what they're doing. 

And then there are the little comments in rehearsals, too—just these tiny, perfectly timed remarks under their breath, or things disguised as innocent clarifying questions that are actually designed to derail the entire workflow and make me look incompetent in front of the rest of the players. 

And the part that makes it so maddening, the part that probably makes it sound to an outsider like I'm the one who's losing it, is that they always have an excuse ready. They will literally show me printed-out emails or pull up these administrative notes on their phones that supposedly explain why the seating had to change or why the rehearsal time was shifted at the last minute. They have this whole paper trail fabricated to justify it, so if you just looked at the surface, you'd think it was all normal administrative chaos. But I know what it really is. I see right through the emails and the notes. I see the actual intent. 

So, no, I'm not losing my grip on reality. I'm just trapped in a reality where I'm being systematically sabotaged by people who are very good at covering their tracks, and I'm exhausted from being the only one willing to look at the actual facts of it.

No one had any reason to sabotage me back then because I wasn't a threat to anyone's ego. \n\nSo, no, I've never experienced anything like this before. An exaggeration? No. No, I... I really need you to understand that I am not distorting anything here. I'm just trapped in a reality where I'm being systematically sabotaged by people who are very good at covering their tracks, and I'm exhausted from being the only one willing to look at the actual facts of it.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt like someone in your personal life, such as a friend or family member, was trying to sabotage or undermine you?\n\nPatient: No, no, absolutely not. We'll sit on the couch, and she'll make tea, and she'll just let me talk through the score and explain exactly why the ensemble's choices were mathematically and musically incorrect. We've been doing that for, gosh, four years now? We bounce ideas off each other. If I write a tricky marimba part, I send it to him first to make sure the sticking actually makes sense for a human being to play. He gives me honest feedback. He doesn't try to ruin my work. If something is unplayable, he just tells me point-blank that I'd need three hands to play it, and we laugh and I fix it. He doesn't wait until a dress rehearsal to deliberately mess it up just to make me look bad in front of a conductor. \n\nSo, no. A delusion? No, I... I really don't think you're grasping the reality of what I'm dealing with here. I'm not here because I'm imagining things out of thin air. I am here because for almost two years—two entire, exhausting years of my life—I have been completely unable to shake the absolute certainty of what they are doing. It’s not a delusion when you can literally watch it unfold in real time on the podium. 

Right after I won the commission, it was like a switch flipped with a few specific people in the ensemble. And they’re smart about it, that’s the thing. They don’t just stand up in the middle of a run-through and yell that they refuse to play my music. It’s insidious. They started using these seemingly mundane administrative things—like schedule changes and seating choices—to quietly undermine my work. 

I mean, do you have any idea how much a seating choice affects the acoustic balance of a new composition? If you move the principal horns even a few feet, or shift the percussion back, it changes the entire texture and resonance of the piece! And the schedule changes... suddenly a critical string sectional is moved to a Tuesday morning when half the players are exhausted from a gig the night before, completely ruining our momentum. And then there are the little comments in rehearsals. Just these tiny, calculated remarks under their breath about my tempo markings or my phrasing, just loud enough to plant seeds of doubt in the younger players' heads. It is a methodical effort to sabotage the piece from the inside out. 

And I know what they say. Because whenever I try to confront them, or whenever I push back, they always have an alibi ready. They’ll pull up their phones and show me emails from the hall coordinator, or they’ll point to some administrative notes that supposedly explain why the schedule *had* to shift, or why the seating was altered for "stage logistics" or whatever nonsense they come up with. They always have this convenient little paper trail that supposedly explains it all away as just normal, everyday orchestral business. But I know what it really is. I can see right through it. I’ve been living with this certainty for two years, watching them quietly try to dismantle my career note by note, and you can’t just write that off as some sort of delusion.

I... I feel like you didn't really hear what I just said. No, it is not just something I perceive, and it is absolutely based on real actions. I know I literally just went over this with you, like, two seconds ago, but I really need you to understand that this isn't just me projecting something that isn't there. 

Look, for almost two years now—twenty-four exhausting months—I have been completely, utterly unable to shake the certainty of what they are doing. It's not a feeling, it's a fact. It started right after I got the commission. That was the catalyst. Before that, things were fine, but the moment that commission was announced, these few specific people in the ensemble just changed. 

And the actions are real! I just listed them for you! The schedule changes that completely mess up our rehearsal flow, the seating choices that destroy the acoustic balance I spent months writing into the score, those little comments they make under their breath to the younger players... those are real things happening in the physical world, not just in my head. They are actively, quietly undermining my work. 

And yes, I know I just told you about how they always have some email or some administrative note from the hall coordinator to supposedly explain it all away. I know how it looks on paper.
